claim: Spontaneous neuronal activity presents sloppiness, where collective behavior is strongly determined by a small number of parameter combinations (stiff dimensions) while being insensitive to many others (sloppy dimensions).
source: Previous research showed that spontaneous neuronal activity presents sloppiness: the collective behavior is strongly determined by a small number of parameter combinations, defined as 'stiff' dimensions, while it is insensitive to many others ('sloppy' dimensions).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research and is a foundational premise of the study.

claim: Cortical state transitions are determined by changes in stiff parameters associated with the activity of a core of neurons with low responses to stimuli and high centrality within the observed network.
source: We showed that cortical state transitions were determined by changes in stiff parameters associated with the activity of a core of neurons with low responses to stimuli and high centrality within the observed network.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on experimental data analysis.

claim: Stimulus-evoked responses evolve along sloppy dimensions associated with the activity of neurons with low centrality and displaying large ongoing and stimulus-evoked fluctuations without affecting the integrity of the network.
source: In contrast, stimulus-evoked responses evolved along sloppy dimensions associated with the activity of neurons with low centrality and displaying large ongoing and stimulus-evoked fluctuations without affecting the integrity of the network.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on experimental data analysis.

claim: Sloppiness is a property of complex models exhibiting large parameter uncertainty when fit to data, meaning that different combinations of parameters lead to similar system behavior.
source: In general, sloppiness is a property of complex models exhibiting large parameter uncertainty when fit to data, meaning that different combinations of parameters lead to a similar system behavior, while changes in some few critical parameters, called stiff parameters, significantly modifies it.
evidence: This is a definition based on established scientific knowledge and cited literature.

claim: Changes in stiff parameters significantly modify system behavior.
source: In general, sloppiness is a property of complex models exhibiting large parameter uncertainty when fit to data, meaning that different combinations of parameters lead to a similar system behavior, while changes in some few critical parameters, called stiff parameters, significantly modifies it.
evidence: This is a definition based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: The spontaneous activity of neural circuits presents sloppiness both in vitro and in vivo.
source: Recently, it has been shown that the spontaneous activity of neural circuits presents sloppiness both in vitro and in vivo (Panas et al., 2015), suggesting that collective activity is stabilized by a subset of highly active and stable neurons, while the activity and co-activity of the remaining neurons present larger spontaneous fluctuations without strongly affecting the collective statistics.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Panas et al., 2015.

claim: Collective activity is stabilized by a subset of highly active and stable neurons, while the activity and co-activity of the remaining neurons present larger spontaneous fluctuations without strongly affecting the collective statistics.
source: Recently, it has been shown that the spontaneous activity of neural circuits presents sloppiness both in vitro and in vivo (Panas et al., 2015), suggesting that collective activity is stabilized by a subset of highly active and stable neurons, while the activity and co-activity of the remaining neurons present larger spontaneous fluctuations without strongly affecting the collective statistics.
evidence: This is a suggestion based on cited research.

claim: Spontaneous cortical activity transits through different synchronized and desynchronized cortical states.
source: However, this view is challenged by extensive research showing that the spontaneous cortical activity transits through different synchronized and desynchronized cortical states (Marguet and Harris, 2011; Harris and Thiele, 2011; Luczak et al., 2013; Pachitariu et al., 2015) that represent statistically different collective behaviors (Hahn et al., 2017) with different information processing capabilities (Pachitariu et al., 2015; Engel et al., 2016; Beaman et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Different synchronized and desynchronized cortical states represent statistically different collective behaviors.
source: However, this view is challenged by extensive research showing that the spontaneous cortical activity transits through different synchronized and desynchronized cortical states (Marguet and Harris, 2011; Harris and Thiele, 2011; Luczak et al., 2013; Pachitariu et al., 2015) that represent statistically different collective behaviors (Hahn et al., 2017) with different information processing capabilities (Pachitariu et al., 2015; Engel et al., 2016; Beaman et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hahn et al., 2017.

claim: Different synchronized and desynchronized cortical states have different information processing capabilities.
source: However, this view is challenged by extensive research showing that the spontaneous cortical activity transits through different synchronized and desynchronized cortical states (Marguet and Harris, 2011; Harris and Thiele, 2011; Luczak et al., 2013; Pachitariu et al., 2015) that represent statistically different collective behaviors (Hahn et al., 2017) with different information processing capabilities (Pachitariu et al., 2015; Engel et al., 2016; Beaman et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Pachitariu et al., 2015; Engel et al., 2016; Beaman et al., 2017.

claim: Neuronal spiking activity was recorded in the primary auditory cortex (A1) of six anesthetized rats.
source: To answer these questions, we recorded the neuronal spiking activity in the primary auditory cortex (A1) of six anesthetized rats.
evidence: This describes the experimental setup and data collection.

claim: The joint activity of groups of neurons was analyzed while the cortex spontaneously transited through different synchronized and desynchronized cortical states and intermittently received external acoustic stimuli.
source: We analyzed the joint activity of groups of neurons while the cortex spontaneously transited through different synchronized and desynchronized cortical states and intermittently received external acoustic stimuli.
evidence: This describes the experimental conditions during data analysis.

claim: A statistical model was used to describe the joint spiking activity with a small number of parameters.
source: We used a statistical model to describe the joint spiking activity with a small number of parameters.
evidence: This describes the analytical method used in the study.

claim: The estimated parameters of neuronal ensemble activity presented sloppiness.
source: We found that the estimated parameters of neuronal ensemble activity presented sloppiness and that sensory inputs and cortical state transitions evolved in different pathways in parameter space.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on data analysis.

claim: Sensory inputs and cortical state transitions evolved in different pathways in parameter space.
source: We found that the estimated parameters of neuronal ensemble activity presented sloppiness and that sensory inputs and cortical state transitions evolved in different pathways in parameter space.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on data analysis.

claim: Cortical state transitions evolve along stiff dimensions.
source: Specifically, we found that cortical state transitions evolve along stiff dimensions, whereas sensory-evoked activity evolves along sloppy dimensions.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on data analysis.

claim: Sensory-evoked activity evolves along sloppy dimensions.
source: Specifically, we found that cortical state transitions evolve along stiff dimensions, whereas sensory-evoked activity evolves along sloppy dimensions.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on data analysis.

claim: Stiff parameters are related to the activity and co-activity of neurons with high centrality within the functional network of the recorded neurons.
source: Finally, we showed that stiff parameters are related to the activity and co-activity of neurons with high centrality within the functional network of the recorded neurons.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on data analysis.

claim: Acoustic 'clicks' were 5-ms square pulses with inter-stimulus interval of 2.5 or 3.5 s.
source: We analyzed the data during spontaneous activity and in response to acoustic 'clicks' (5-ms square pulses; inter-stimulus interval, 2.5 or 3.5 s).
evidence: This describes the stimulus parameters used in the experiment.

claim: Spontaneous activity was defined as the activity during 1.5-s intervals preceding each stimulus.
source: Within each 100-s epoch the data was separated into spontaneous activity, that is the activity during 1.5-s intervals preceding each stimulus (i.e., 18–43.5 s of spontaneous activity in total for each epoch), and stimulus-evoked activity, that is the activity right after the stimulus onset (Figure 1A–B).
evidence: This defines the operational definition of spontaneous activity used in the study.

claim: Stimulus-evoked activity was defined as the activity right after the stimulus onset.
source: Within each 100-s epoch the data was separated into spontaneous activity, that is the activity during 1.5-s intervals preceding each stimulus (i.e., 18–43.5 s of spontaneous activity in total for each epoch), and stimulus-evoked activity, that is the activity right after the stimulus onset (Figure 1A–B).
evidence: This defines the operational definition of stimulus-evoked activity used in the study.

claim: Time was discretized in bins of dt = 10 ms for the maximum entropy model.
source: To fit the model, time was discretized in bins of dt = 10 ms.
evidence: This describes a methodological parameter of the analysis.

claim: The model parameters substantially changed over time.
source: Indeed, the model parameters substantially changed over time, with a rapidly decaying similarity (Figure 3C, orange and purple traces).
evidence: This is a finding from the temporal analysis, supported by Figure 3C.

claim: The FIM had the highest stability across time, compared to the data firing rates and correlations and the model parameters.
source: We first notice that the FIM had the highest stability across time, compared to the data firing rates and correlations and the model parameters (Figure 3C, blue trace).
evidence: This is a finding from the temporal analysis, supported by Figure 3C.

claim: The sensitivity of the model parameters remained relatively stable despite substantial changes in firing rates, correlations, collective activity and the model parameters themselves.
source: Altogether these results show that the sensitivity of the model parameters remained relatively stable despite substantial changes in firing rates, correlations, collective activity and the model parameters themselves.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the temporal analysis results.

claim: Most elements of the FIM had near-zero values indicating that most of the parameters had a small effect on the model log-likelihood.
source: First, we noted that most elements of the FIM had near-zero values (Figure 4A) indicating that most of the parameters had a small effect on the model log-likelihood.
evidence: This is a finding from the FIM analysis, supported by Figure 4A.

claim: A small fraction of FIM elements had values strongly different from zero as revealed by the heavy tail of the distribution of FIM values.
source: In contrast, a small fraction of elements had values strongly different from zero as revealed by the heavy tail of the distribution of FIM values (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a finding from the FIM analysis, supported by Figure 4A.

claim: Most of the FIM eigenvalues were small, corresponding to combinations of parameters that had little effect on model behavior (sloppy dimensions).
source: We observed that, except for some few eigenvalues, most of the FIM eigenvalues were small, corresponding to combinations of parameters that had little effect on model behavior. These unimportant parameter combinations defined the sloppy dimensions of the model.
evidence: This is a finding from the eigenvalue decomposition of the FIM, shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The few eigenvectors with large eigenvalues defined the stiff parameter dimensions along which the model behavior was strongly affected.
source: The few eigenvectors with large eigenvalues defined the stiff parameter dimensions along which the model behavior was strongly affected.
evidence: This is a finding from the eigenvalue decomposition of the FIM, shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The projection variance increased as a function of the eigenvector's rank for all datasets.
source: We found that the projection variance increased as a function of the eigenvector's rank for all datasets (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is a finding from the parameter projection analysis, supported by Figure 4E.

claim: Parameter fluctuations were not fully explained by estimation errors.
source: Using stationary surrogate data, we controlled that these parameter fluctuations were not fully explained by estimation errors and, furthermore, that parameter fluctuations along sloppy dimensions were those that deviated the most from the stationary case (see Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the surrogate data analysis, supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Parameter fluctuations along sloppy dimensions were those that deviated the most from the stationary case.
source: Using stationary surrogate data, we controlled that these parameter fluctuations were not fully explained by estimation errors and, furthermore, that parameter fluctuations along sloppy dimensions were those that deviated the most from the stationary case (see Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the surrogate data analysis, supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The projection variance into the stiff dimensions, albeit small, was not zero.
source: Nevertheless, we noted that the projection variance into the stiff dimensions, albeit small, was not zero.
evidence: This is an observation from the parameter projection analysis.

claim: The model also evolved along parameter dimensions that had a strong impact on the collective activity.
source: This means that the model also evolved along parameter dimensions that had a strong impact on the collective activity.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that projection variance into stiff dimensions was not zero.

claim: Changes in collective behavior, associated to changes in stiff parameters, were related to changes in cortical state.
source: We hypothesized that changes in collective behavior, associated to changes in stiff parameters, were related to changes in cortical state.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their observations.

claim: Low and high values of silence density were associated to desynchronized and synchronized cortical states, respectively.
source: During the course of the experiment, we observed large fluctuations in silence density, with low and high values associated to desynchronized and synchronized cortical states, respectively (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a finding from the cortical state analysis, supported by Figure 5A.

claim: Changes in collective behavior correlated with changes in cortical state.
source: Thus, changes in collective behavior correlated with changes in cortical state.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the correlation analysis.

claim: The observables that correlated more with the cortical state were those with the highest associated sensitivity.
source: Thus, the observables that correlated more with the cortical state were those with the highest associated sensitivity.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the correlation analysis.

claim: Stiff variables were significantly more correlated with the cortical state than the sloppy variables (p<0.01 for all datasets, paired t-test).
source: We found that stiff variables were significantly more correlated with the cortical state than the sloppy variables (p<0.01 for all datasets, paired t-test; Figure 5G).
evidence: This is a finding from statistical comparison, supported by Figure 5G.

claim: Neuronal activity and co-activity preferentially evolved along sensitive (stiff) parameter dimensions during cortical state transitions.
source: Altogether, these results indicate that neuronal activity and co-activity preferentially evolved along sensitive (stiff) parameter dimensions during cortical state transitions.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the cortical state analysis.

claim: Evoked responses were larger for sloppy neurons than for stiff neurons.
source: We observed that evoked responses (which could be increased or decreased with respect to pre-stimulus baseline firing rate) were larger for sloppy neurons than for stiff neurons (Figure 6B–C).
evidence: This is a finding from the stimulus response analysis, supported by Figures 6B-C.

claim: The more responsive neurons were those with the lowest associated sensitivity.
source: We found that the more responsive neurons were those with the lowest associated sensitivity (Figure 6D–E).
evidence: This is a finding from the modulation index analysis, supported by Figures 6D-E.

claim: Stimulus-evoked neuronal activity evolved mostly along sloppy dimensions.
source: This indicates that stimulus-evoked neuronal activity evolved mostly along sloppy dimensions.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the modulation index analysis.

claim: ΔMI was maximal during desynchronized activity, and minimal during synchronized activity.
source: We found that ΔMI was maximal during desynchronized activity, and minimal during synchronized activity (Figure 6F, see also Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a finding from the state-dependent analysis, supported by Figure 6F.

claim: The cortical activity during stimulus response evolved predominantly along sloppy dimensions for the desynchronized cortical state, while, in the synchronized state, the dominance of sloppy fluctuations was reduced, and stiff fluctuations became comparable.
source: Thus, the cortical activity during stimulus response evolved predominantly along sloppy dimensions for the desynchronized cortical state, while, in the synchronized state, the dominance of sloppy fluctuations was reduced, and stiff fluctuations became comparable.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the state-dependent analysis.

claim: Stiff units were significantly more active than sloppy units (AUC = 0.961–0.998, p < 0.001, for all rats).
source: With this dichotomization, we found that stiff units were significantly more active than sloppy units (Figure 7A). We quantified this by performing receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis and used the area under the ROC curve (AUC) as a measure of how well the firing rates distributions of the two classes were separated (AUC = 0.961–0.998, p < 0.001, for all rats; Figure 7G).
evidence: This is a finding from the ROC analysis, supported by Figures 7A and 7G.

claim: Stiff neurons were significantly more correlated among them than sloppy neurons (AUC = 0.615–0.932, p < 0.001, for all rats).
source: Stiff neurons were also significantly more correlated among them than sloppy neurons (AUC = 0.615–0.932, p < 0.001, for all rats; Figure 7B,G).
evidence: This is a finding from the ROC analysis, supported by Figures 7B and 7G.

claim: Stiff neurons had significantly more centrality in the functional connectivity graph than sloppy neurons (AUC = 0.740–0.831, p<0.001, for all rats).
source: We found that stiff neurons had significantly more centrality in the functional connectivity graph than sloppy neurons (AUC = 0.740–0.831, p<0.001, for all rats; Figure 7D,G).
evidence: This is a finding from the betweenness centrality analysis, supported by Figures 7D and 7G.

claim: Stiff neurons were part of the core of the graph, while sloppy neurons were part of the graph periphery.
source: This indicates that stiff neurons were part of the core of the graph, while sloppy neurons were part of the graph periphery, as clearly shown using graph visualization (Figure 7E; Fruchterman and Reingold, 1991).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the centrality analysis, supported by Figure 7E and cited visualization method.

claim: BC values were correlated with firing rates (correlation coefficient: 0.59 ± 0.11).
source: BC values were correlated with firing rates (correlation coefficient: 0.59 ± 0.11), which could suggest that differences in BC between stiff and sloppy neurons were simply a consequence of differences in firing rates.
evidence: This is a finding from correlation analysis.

claim: Neither the structure of correlations nor the BC values could be trivially predicted by globally modulated firing rates but they were rather suggestive of functional interactions.
source: However, using surrogate data that preserved the observed firing rates and produced correlations through global modulations, we found that neither the structure of correlations nor the BC values could be trivially predicted by globally modulated firing rates but they were rather suggestive of functional interactions (see Appendix 1 and Appendix 1—figure 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the surrogate data analysis, supported by Appendix 1 and Appendix 1—figure 2.

claim: Different firing rates, different correlations and BC values were supplementary features of stiff and sloppy neurons.
source: Thus, in addition to different firing rates, different correlations and BC values were supplementary features of stiff and sloppy neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the analysis of neuron properties.

claim: Stiff neurons were significantly more coupled to the population activity than sloppy neurons (AUC = 0.603–0.939, p < 0.001, for all rats).
source: We found that stiff neurons were significantly more coupled to the population activity than sloppy neurons (AUC = 0.603–0.939, p < 0.001, for all rats; Figure 7F,G).
evidence: This is a finding from the neuron-to-population coupling analysis, supported by Figures 7F and 7G.

claim: Stiff units were more active, more central, more coupled among them, and more coupled to the population activity than sloppy units.
source: In summary, stiff units were more active, more central, more coupled among them, and more coupled to the population activity than sloppy units.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings about stiff vs. sloppy neuron properties.

claim: A stimulus can modulate the activity of a subset of sloppy neurons without entirely affecting the collective activity.
source: It suggests that a stimulus can modulate the activity of a subset of sloppy neurons without entirely affecting the collective activity.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the functional implications of the findings.

claim: This could be an efficient functional architecture to encode sensory information without perturbing other ongoing or memory-stored processes.
source: This could be an efficient functional architecture to encode sensory information without perturbing other ongoing or memory-stored processes.
evidence: This is a speculation about the functional significance of the findings.

claim: The integrity of the network is ensured by a core of highly active stiff neurons, which have strong functional connections among them, while topologically peripheral sloppy neurons can be largely modulated by external inputs.
source: Consistent with this view and with previous studies (Margolis et al., 2012; Mizuseki and Buzsáki, 2013; Panas et al., 2015), our results suggest that the integrity of the network is ensured by a core of highly active stiff neurons, which have strong functional connections among them (either through anatomical connections or common inputs), while topologically peripheral sloppy neurons (within the functional connectivity graph) can be largely modulated by external inputs.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings, supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: A similar sub-network of highly active, interconnected neurons has been recently identified in the mice neocortex.
source: A similar sub-network of highly active, interconnected neurons has been recently identified in the mice neocortex (Yassin et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a citation to related findings in other research.

claim: Sensory input was not required to drive these cells.
source: Importantly, sensory input was not required to drive these cells.
evidence: This is a statement about the properties of the neurons identified in the cited study.

claim: The network periphery is more variable, evolvable, and plastic than the network core, while the network core facilitates system robustness.
source: Previous studies of complex systems have derived general principles of core/periphery network structures: the network periphery is more variable, evolvable, and plastic than the network core, while the network core facilitates system robustness (Kitano, 2004; Csermely et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a general principle from complex systems theory, supported by citations.

claim: Sloppy neurons could be more affected by synaptic plasticity, allowing for network reconfiguration without loss of stability.
source: Thus, we hypothesize that sloppy neurons could also be more affected by synaptic plasticity, allowing for network reconfiguration without loss of stability.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their findings and general principles.

claim: Previous work on whole-brain fMRI has observed core stability and peripheral flexibility over the course of learning.
source: Consistent with this, previous work on whole-brain fMRI has observed core stability and peripheral flexibility over the course of learning (Bassett et al., 2013), and recent analyses of functional networks from calcium imaging data recorded in mouse primary auditory cortex revealed a stable core and a variable periphery over time (Betzel et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a citation to related findings in other research.

claim: Recent analyses of functional networks from calcium imaging data recorded in mouse primary auditory cortex revealed a stable core and a variable periphery over time.
source: Consistent with this, previous work on whole-brain fMRI has observed core stability and peripheral flexibility over the course of learning (Bassett et al., 2013), and recent analyses of functional networks from calcium imaging data recorded in mouse primary auditory cortex revealed a stable core and a variable periphery over time (Betzel et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a citation to related findings in other research.

claim: Stimulus responses evolved more pronouncedly along sloppy dimensions in the desynchronized state, while in the synchronized state fluctuations along sloppy and stiff dimensions were comparable.
source: Furthermore, we observed that stimulus responses evolved more pronouncedly along sloppy dimensions in the desynchronized state, while in the synchronized state fluctuations along sloppy and stiff dimensions were comparable (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is a finding from the state-dependent analysis, supported by Figure 6F.

claim: Responses along sloppy dimensions provide information processing benefits.
source: This supports the view that responses along sloppy dimensions provide information processing benefits, since previous studies have shown that auditory stimuli in rodents (Marguet and Harris, 2011; Pachitariu et al., 2015) and visual stimuli in both rats (Goard and Dan, 2009) and monkeys (Beaman et al., 2017) are better represented in the desynchronized state as compared to the synchronized state.
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Auditory stimuli in rodents are better represented in the desynchronized state as compared to the synchronized state.
source: This supports the view that responses along sloppy dimensions provide information processing benefits, since previous studies have shown that auditory stimuli in rodents (Marguet and Harris, 2011; Pachitariu et al., 2015) and visual stimuli in both rats (Goard and Dan, 2009) and monkeys (Beaman et al., 2017) are better represented in the desynchronized state as compared to the synchronized state.
evidence: This is a citation to previous research findings.

claim: Visual stimuli in both rats and monkeys are better represented in the desynchronized state as compared to the synchronized state.
source: This supports the view that responses along sloppy dimensions provide information processing benefits, since previous studies have shown that auditory stimuli in rodents (Marguet and Harris, 2011; Pachitariu et al., 2015) and visual stimuli in both rats (Goard and Dan, 2009) and monkeys (Beaman et al., 2017) are better represented in the desynchronized state as compared to the synchronized state.
evidence: This is a citation to previous research findings.

claim: The properties of spontaneous and induced cortical dynamics observed in the present anesthetized condition are likely to be relevant also during wakefulness.
source: The properties of spontaneous and induced cortical dynamics observed in the present anesthetized condition are likely to be relevant also during wakefulness.
evidence: This is a speculation about the generalizability of the findings.

claim: Several studies reported the existence of synchronized cortical states during wakefulness.
source: Indeed, several studies reported the existence of synchronized cortical states during wakefulness (for review see Zagha and McCormick, 2014), and global fluctuation resembling transitions between up and down periods during alert or quiescent wakefulness (Petersen et al., 2003; Luczak et al., 2007; Poulet and Petersen, 2008; Zagha et al., 2013; Tan et al., 2014; Engel et al., 2016) or even during task engagement (Sachidhanandam et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a citation to previous research findings.

claim: Global fluctuation resembling transitions between up and down periods occur during alert or quiescent wakefulness.
source: Indeed, several studies reported the existence of synchronized cortical states during wakefulness (for review see Zagha and McCormick, 2014), and global fluctuation resembling transitions between up and down periods during alert or quiescent wakefulness (Petersen et al., 2003; Luczak et al., 2007; Poulet and Petersen, 2008; Zagha et al., 2013; Tan et al., 2014; Engel et al., 2016) or even during task engagement (Sachidhanandam et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a citation to previous research findings.

claim: Global fluctuation resembling transitions between up and down periods occur even during task engagement.
source: Indeed, several studies reported the existence of synchronized cortical states during wakefulness (for review see Zagha and McCormick, 2014), and global fluctuation resembling transitions between up and down periods during alert or quiescent wakefulness (Petersen et al., 2003; Luczak et al., 2007; Poulet and Petersen, 2008; Zagha et al., 2013; Tan et al., 2014; Engel et al., 2016) or even during task engagement (Sachidhanandam et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a citation to previous research findings.

claim: Sloppiness has been observed in asynchronous spontaneous activity under light anesthesia.
source: Moreover, sloppiness has been observed in asynchronous spontaneous activity under light anesthesia (Panas et al., 2015), we thus expect to observe a similar stiff-sloppy architecture in the awake state.
evidence: This is a citation to previous research findings.

claim: We expect to observe a similar stiff-sloppy architecture in the awake state.
source: Moreover, sloppiness has been observed in asynchronous spontaneous activity under light anesthesia (Panas et al., 2015), we thus expect to observe a similar stiff-sloppy architecture in the awake state.
evidence: This is a speculation based on previous findings.

claim: The comparison of Fisher information matrices during wakefulness and during different levels of anesthesia could provide valuable information about the principles governing vigilance.
source: However, we believe that the comparison of Fisher information matrices during wakefulness and during different levels of anesthesia could provide valuable information about the principles governing vigilance.
evidence: This is a speculation about future research directions.

claim: Stiff neurons were more linked to the observed neuronal population activity than sloppy neurons.
source: We found that stiff neurons were more linked to the observed neuronal population activity than sloppy neurons.
evidence: This is a summary of findings about neuron properties.

claim: Stiff neurons had higher centrality in the functional connectivity graph and higher coupling to the population activity than sloppy neurons.
source: Stiff neurons had higher centrality in the functional connectivity graph and higher coupling to the population activity than sloppy neurons.
evidence: This is a summary of findings about neuron properties.

claim: Neurons differ in their coupling to the population activity, with neurons that activate most often when many others are active (choristers) and neurons that tend to activate more frequently when others are silent (soloists).
source: Previous research showed that neurons differ in their coupling to the population activity, with neurons that activate most often when many others are active, called 'choristers', and neurons that tend to activate more frequently when others are silent, called 'soloists' (Okun et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a citation to previous research findings.

claim: Stiff and sloppy neurons are chorister and soloist neurons, respectively.
source: Our results suggest that stiff and sloppy neurons are chorister and soloist neurons, respectively.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in relation to previous concepts.

claim: Changes in the activity of stiff/chorister neurons lead to changes in collective behavior (i.e., cortical states), while the activity of sloppy/soloist neurons can spontaneously fluctuate or respond to stimuli without strongly affecting the collective behavior.
source: In other words, changes in the activity of stiff/chorister neurons lead to changes in collective behavior (i.e., cortical states), while the activity of sloppy/soloist neurons can spontaneously fluctuate or respond to stimuli without strongly affecting the collective behavior.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the functional roles of different neuron types.

claim: The roles of stiff/chorister neurons and sloppy/soloist neurons are important to understand tradeoffs between responsiveness and stability of the network.
source: Thus, we believe that the roles of stiff/chorister neurons and sloppy/soloist neurons are important to understand tradeoffs between responsiveness and stability of the network.
evidence: This is a speculation about the functional significance of the findings.

claim: Fluctuations on stiff parameter dimensions were the weakest and were related to cortical state transitions, which time scale is in the order of tens of minutes.
source: Furthermore, we here studied the evolution of neuronal activity on the time scale of hours and found that fluctuations on stiff parameter dimensions were the weakest and were related to cortical state transitions, which time scale is in the order of tens of minutes (Hahn et al., 2017; Mochol et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a finding from the temporal analysis, supported by citations.

claim: Previous studies have reported prominent changes on neuronal activity and tuning properties over days, but with stable decoding performances of population activity.
source: Previous studies have reported prominent changes on neuronal activity and tuning properties over days, but with stable decoding performances of population activity (Chestek et al., 2007; Ziv et al., 2013; Panas et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a citation to previous research findings.

claim: Learning or adaptation to changing environments could lead to large changes in collective activity.
source: However, we hypothesize that learning or adaptation to changing environments could lead to large changes in collective activity.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: Top-down regulation might be a mechanism to control the stabilizing network core.
source: In that case, particular attention could be paid to the influence of high-order areas on the activity of subsets of stiff and sloppy neurons from sensory areas, as top-down regulation might be a mechanism to control the stabilizing network core.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential mechanisms.

claim: The existence of cortical neurons with different sensitivities (from sloppy to stiff neurons) provides new valuable architectural constrains for models of the brain state and its transitions.
source: The existence of cortical neurons with different sensitivities (from sloppy to stiff neurons) provides new valuable architectural constrains for models of the brain state and its transitions.
evidence: This is a statement about the implications of the findings for modeling.

claim: Several past studies have modeled the synchronized brain dynamics as transitions between two attractors.
source: Several past studies have modeled the synchronized brain dynamics as transitions between two attractors. Depending on the model specificity those transitions could be noise driven (Mejias et al., 2010; Mochol et al., 2015; Jercog et al., 2017) or caused by some fatigue mechanism (Compte et al., 2003; Hill and Tononi, 2005; Mattia and Sanchez-Vives, 2012).
evidence: This is a citation to previous modeling approaches.

claim: To make the system work in a desynchronized regime it was enough to increase the background input to the network.
source: To make the system works in a desynchronized regime it was enough to increase the background input to the network (Bazhenov et al., 2002; Hill and Tononi, 2005; Curto et al., 2009; Destexhe, 2009; Mochol et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a citation to previous modeling approaches.

claim: The models could be extended to include a network core/periphery architecture, a non-homogeneous background input preferentially targeting the network core, and different stimulus spatial distributions.
source: Given our present results, the models could be extended to include a network core/periphery architecture, a non-homogeneous background input preferentially targeting the network core, and different stimulus spatial distributions.
